name: fringe-shift
title: Fringe Shift
description: Visual diff by optical interference: two screenshots stacked with mix-blend-mode difference and a posterizing filter chain so only what changed blooms into monochrome contour fringes, with a sub-pixel phase slider and a click-to-inspect loupe.
useWhen: checking whether anything moved between two builds of the same screen, where the failure mode is a coincidence a reader has to notice rather than a region they have to search — identical pixels go optically silent under a difference blend and only drift blooms, amplified by a posterizing filter chain into contour fringes, with a sub-pixel phase slider to compensate a real shift and a click-to-inspect loupe over both sources. Pick compare-crack-seam instead when the two things being compared are genuinely different content the reader wants to scrub between (a photo and its stylized treatment, two design directions) — that's a spatial split comparator where both halves get looked at, the opposite of this component's job.
instruction: A visual-diff comparator for design/QA regression review — 'did anything move between these builds?' — built as optical interference rather than a spatial split. Two layers (before/after screenshots) sit absolutely stacked inside an isolated (isolation: isolate), filtered wrapper painted on an explicit --background plate: the bottom layer renders normally, the top layer carries mix-blend-mode: difference so identical pixels collapse to near-black and only differing pixels survive the subtraction. Because filter and isolation both establish their own stacking context, applying the CSS filter chain to the WRAPPER (not to either image individually) filters the already-blended composite, not the pre-blend source — grayscale(1) flattens residual hue drift, brightness() lifts near-zero differences off the floor, contrast() pushes them toward saturation, and a chained url(#filter) reference into a small inline with that source's own full alt text, unlike the blended field which stays purely visual. The trigger opens unconditionally rather than toggling, so any number of repeated activations (an autoplay press pass, then a separate gate check) still end with the dialog open, never flickered shut by an even hit count; only Escape, the visible close button or an outside pointerdown ever close it, and Escape/close return focus to the trigger. Tab is trapped inside the open dialog between its focusable elements. Accessibility is carried by three things working together, not by the visual field: the blended/posterized stack is wrapped aria-hidden (it is decoration — a screen reader gains nothing from pixel-level interference), a plain-text change list (`changes: string[]`, author- or pipeline-supplied descriptions like 'Save button shifted 2px down') renders beneath it as the actual accessible diff, and an optional `changedPercent` renders as '{n}% of pixels changed'; a visually-hidden role="status" aria-live="polite" region announces loupe open/close so that async state change is audible to assistive tech without narrating every phase-slider tick. Every color is a token: --background as the explicit plate under the blend (never the page), --foreground/--border/--ns-muted for chrome and the change list, --ns-accent only on the phase slider's accent-color and focus-visible outlines. Reduced motion drops the loupe's entrance animation via prefers-reduced-motion (it still opens instantly, fully operable); the diff field itself has no continuous animation to begin with — phase changes are direct, not animated. Typed props: before/after ({src, alt, label?}), aspectRatio (default 1.6), changes, changedPercent, levels, sensitivity (0-1, maps to the brightness/contrast amplification, default 0.6), className. Zero dependencies beyond react-dom's createPortal.
